lesson.title: Numbers, Time & gestern
lesson.subtitle: Counting is a shift spiral: drei↔three, zwanzig↔twenty, dreißig↔thirty

hook.title: The Counting Spiral
hook.content: Numbers look like the least poetic words in any language — and German numbers are secretly the whole curriculum in miniature. drei is three (TH→D). zwanzig is twenty (TW→ZW). dreißig is thirty (TH→D and T→ß in one word — a double-shift number). elf is eleven — both from 'one left over' after ten. And the time words keep spiraling: gestern ↔ yesterday (the y- and g- are one letter in two fonts), heute is 'on this day' (the heu- is the he- of here), morgen the morrow of to-morrow. You have been counting German since childhood — today you just get the credit.

footnotes.title: The 'Left Over' Numbers
footnotes.content: Eleven and twelve are the most honest numbers in Germanic: *ainalif 'one-left' and *twalif 'two-left' — what remains when you have counted up to ten on both hands. German elf and zwölf keep the arithmetic visible; English eleven and twelve wore it smooth.

pattern.title: Count, Tell Time, Name the Day
pattern.content: Counting: drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben (seven, v→b), acht (eight, the gh→ch word), neun, zehn — the middle ones (vier, fünf, sechs, neun, zehn) arrive as vocab hints today and formal cognates later. Bigger: zwanzig (twenty), dreißig (thirty — note the ß: thirty is the one number that spelled its shift), elf (eleven), zwölf (twelve). Compound numbers put the ones first, like archaic English 'five-and-twenty': dreiundzwanzig. Time: Es ist drei Uhr — Uhr is the loan-twin of hour. Days wear the shift: Donnerstag (thunder-day), Mittwoch (mid-week), and the calendar trio gestern — heute — morgen runs yesterday–today–tomorrow with every pair a cognate.
pattern.linguist_note: gestern and yesterday are the same y→g word: English yester- survives only in yesterday and yesteryear, while German gestern stayed in daily use. The g of gestern is exactly the g of sagen (say) — English vocalized it, German kept it.

exercises.prompt: Match the shifted numbers with their English twins:
exercises.explanation: TH→D in drei, TW→ZW in zwölf and zwanzig, and a double shift in dreißig — counting runs the whole shift ledger. Even moving day runs on numbers: um acht Uhr wollen wir ausziehen — the separable verb from the routine lessons rides the clock.

exercises.prompt: German 'elf' means eleven. What did the word originally describe?
options: One left over (after counting all ten fingers)
exercises.target_answer: One left over (after counting all ten fingers)
exercises.explanation: *ainalif, 'one left' — and zwölf is *twalif, 'two left'. The numbers are honest arithmetic from ten fingers.
German compounds ones before tens, the way archaic English said 'five-and-twenty' — one word, no hyphens.

exercises.prompt: What English time word is the twin of 'gestern'?
exercises.explanation: gestern ↔ yester-: the same word with y→g. English retired it into 'yesterday'; German kept it standalone.

exercises.idea: someone stops you on the street and asks the time: it is three o'clock
cues: The clock formula is a twin sandwich: es ↔ it, ist ↔ is, drei ↔ three, Uhr ↔ hour — Es ist drei Uhr
exercises.affirmation: You built the clock sentence from four twins — es, ist, drei, Uhr: English with a German accent.

vocab_hints.note: loan-twin of hour; o'clock is literally 'of the clock'

exercises.explanation: Es ist drei Uhr — the es ↔ it twin opening the clock formula, built from a thought.

summary.outcome: Count to 30+, tell clock time, and use the gestern–heute–morgen calendar trio.
summary.takeaway: Numbers carry the whole shift ledger — drei, zwölf, zwanzig, dreißig — and the time words are pure cognates.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the counting cognates gym — phone numbers, prices, ages, and the elf≠elf trap.

twist.prompt: Same clock, lunchtime: it is three o'clock becomes it is TWELVE o'clock. (The number carries the shift ledger.)
twist.explanation: Only the number changes: zwölf is your twelve in shift clothes (the tw → zw opener from the early trail). The clock formula never moves.

zwanzig.etymology_derivation: zwei + -zig (German's ancient -ty, as in six-ty); the whole word is a double t → z shift of twenty. [wiktionary]

elf.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *ainalif — 'one left over' after counting ten, the exact twin of eleven. [wiktionary]

zwölf.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *twalif — 'two left over', the exact tw → zw twin of twelve. [wiktionary]

dreißig.shift_rule: TH → D + T → S / SS / Z
dreißig.etymology_derivation: drei + the old -zig ending (English's -ty): thirty with th → d and t → ß — a double-shift number. [wiktionary]

morgen.etymology_derivation: Cognate with English morrow (hence to-morrow) and morn — both descend from the Germanic root for "morning". [wiktionary]

heute.etymology_derivation: Literally 'on this day': heu- is the he- of here/him, and the old ending hid Tag (day). English's own twin hēodæġ died out — today won. [wiktionary]

uhr.etymology_derivation: Loan-cognate of hour (Latin hōra via French), and a distant doublet of Jahr and year (PIE *yóh₁r̥). German alone turned it into the word for the clock itself. [wiktionary]

donner.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Living in English "Thursday" (Thor's/Thunder's day = Donnerstag) and Santa's reindeer "Donner and Blitzen" (Thunder and Lightning).

woche.context_phrase: Nächste Woche fahre ich nach Berlin.
woche.context_translation: Next week I travel to Berlin.

zehe.context_phrase: Ich habe mir die Zehe gestoßen.

schwitzen.context_translation: In summer, we sweat a lot.
schwitzen.etymology_derivation: From Old High German swizzen, from Proto-West Germanic *swittjan, from Proto-Germanic *switjaną. English sweat is a listed cognate. [wiktionary]

uhrzeit.etymology_derivation: Uhr + Zeit — clock-time; Zeit is the twin of English tide, which originally meant time, as in eventide. [wiktionary]

lassen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *lētaną via Proto-West Germanic *lātan — English let is the documented cognate; the old t survives in English but hissed to ss in German. Strong verb: ließ, gelassen. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
